title: Stage 10: 1B users
scopeHtml: Scope: cells, capacity planning, cost, migrations at scale, chaos testing, abuse and security, org structure. Questions are still to be written.

notes.title: Load and goal
notes.html:
Stage 10 goal: at 1B registered users (about 400M DAU), keep Chirp fast, safe, affordable and changeable, even though no single change can be tested on a full copy of production. The enemy is no longer a bottleneck; it is blast radius, cost per user and the speed of the organisation.

Quantity Value
Registered / DAU 1B / 400M
Timeline reads 8B/day = 93k/s avg, 280k/s peak (global events: 3 to 5x)
Posts 200M/day = 2,300/s avg, 10k/s peak, up to 30k/s during a world event
Fan-out writes 200M x 100 = 20B/day = 230k/s avg (hybrid keeps this finite)
Media 50M/day x 600 KB = 30 TB/day, 11 PB/year
Engineers 800 to 1,500 in about 100 teams
Budget infrastructure cost per DAU per month must stay under about $0.01

Industry examples. AWS builds services as cells (each region contains many cells, a customer maps to one cell); Slack moved to cell-based architecture after outages in 2021 to 2022; Netflix Chaos Monkey and Simian Army, Gremlin; Uber's DOMA domains; Meta's Cassandra, TAO and ZippyDB; Twitter/X's Manhattan store and Snowflake ids; Amazon's "two-pizza teams" and Conway's law.

Everyday analogy. A ship with watertight compartments: a hole floods one compartment, not the ship.

Common interview traps.

  • Describing "scale" as only more machines; at this stage the interviewer wants blast radius, cost and org.
  • Quoting "1B users" without separating registered, monthly, daily and concurrent.

notes.title: Configuration
notes.html:
Cell-based architecture.

Setting Value
Cell definition a complete, independent copy of the core stack serving a fixed set of users: API pods, Postgres shards, Redis, Kafka, search shard
Cell size about 10M registered users / 4M DAU (about 2,800 reads/s avg; 7k/s peak)
Cells 100 globally (about 35 US, 25 EU, 40 APAC)
Max cell utilisation 60% steady, add a new cell at 50% fill rate
Cell router thin stateless layer at the edge; user_id -> cell from a replicated map (1B x 16 B = 16 GB, kept in a sharded KV with local caches, TTL 10 min)
Shared things (kept few) identity/auth, global username uniqueness, billing, abuse signals, control plane
Data plane vs control plane the control plane (deploys, cell placement) may fail without taking down serving 
# Cell template (one per cell, stamped by Terraform)
cell:
  id: eu-west-1-c07
  api: { nodes: 40, type: c7g.2xlarge, min: 25, max: 80 }
  postgres: { shards: 16, instance: db.r6g.4xlarge, standby: sync, replica: 1 }
  redis: { primaries: 12, type: cache.r7g.2xlarge }
  kafka: { brokers: 6, partitions_posts: 48 }
  search: { data_nodes: 6, type: r6g.2xlarge }
  capacity_alarm: { fill: 0.5 }
  rollout_wave: 3        # deploy waves: wave 0 = canary cell, 1 = 2 cells, 2 = 10, 3 = rest

Capacity planning loop.

  • Forecast: weekly DAU growth (say 0.5%/week), seasonal events (World Cup, elections, New Year's Eve peaks 3 to 5x).
  • Headroom rules: N+1 cell per region, peak x 1.5, plus event buffer.
  • Load test monthly with synthetic replay at 2x peak on a staging cell and on production cells using shadow traffic.
  • Reserved/committed capacity for the baseline (70%), on-demand for peaks (20%), spot for batch (10%).

Chaos testing. Weekly game days; automated experiments in production: kill 1 pod per service per hour (Chaos Mesh/Litmus), inject 200 ms latency on 5% of calls to a dependency, drop an AZ in one cell (quarterly), simulate a region evacuation (twice a year). Steady-state hypothesis: SLO unchanged. Abort conditions: burn rate > 2x.

Abuse and security.

Layer Config
Edge WAF (OWASP rules), bot score, DDoS scrubbing (Cloudflare/Shield Advanced), per-ASN limits
Rate limits per user, per IP, per device fingerprint; adaptive thresholds from ML score
Spam async classifiers on Kafka post.created, p99 decision under 2 s for new accounts, reputation score stored in Redis
Account safety 2FA, new-device challenge, credential-stuffing detection (many logins, many accounts per IP)
Data TLS 1.3 everywhere, mTLS inside, envelope encryption (KMS) per cell, secrets in Vault, rotate every 90 days
Supply chain signed images, SBOM, dependency pinning

Common interview traps.

  • Sizing a cell without a clear rule on what happens when it fills.
  • Chaos testing only in staging; real weaknesses appear in production-like data and traffic.

notes.title: Decision and why
notes.html:
1. Cells instead of one giant regional stack. If a bad deploy or poison request breaks one cell, only 1% of users are affected (blast radius = cell size / total). Testing becomes possible: the cell is a unit you can load test completely. Capacity is added by stamping a new cell, not by resharding a monster. Each cell stays within sizes that the team already understands operationally (16 DB shards, 12 Redis primaries). Scaling stops being a research problem.

2. Deploy in waves by cell. Wave 0: one internal canary cell (employees). Wave 1: 2 small cells. Wave 2: 10 cells across regions. Bake time 30 min to 24 h per wave; automated rollback on SLO burn. A bug thus touches at most 1 to 3% before detection.

3. Capacity planning at the cell level. A known unit with a known cost makes "how much for the next 100M users" trivial: 10 cells x cell cost.

4. Migration at scale (the hard part). Rules:

  • Never big-bang. Use expand/contract plus dual writes plus shadow reads.
  • Online backfill at throttled rates (e.g. 5k rows/s per shard, watch replica lag < 1 s, auto-pause).
  • Verify with checksums and shadow comparison (read both, compare, log diffs) for days before cutover.
  • Cutover by cell/percentage, instant fallback by flipping a flag.
  • Example: moving posts from Postgres to a new store: dual write 100% (week 1), backfill history (weeks 2 to 4), shadow-read 1% to 100% (weeks 5 to 6), read cutover by wave (weeks 7 to 9), stop old writes (week 10), delete old after 30 days.
  • Moving a user between cells (rebalance): freeze writes for that user for 2 to 10 s, copy, flip map entry, unfreeze.

5. Cost control. At this size 5% saved is $400k/month. Levers: ARM Graviton (20 to 30% cheaper per unit work), committed use discounts (30 to 50%), spot for stateless batch, tiered storage (hot 7 days, warm 90 days, cold glacier), AVIF/H.265 for media (30 to 50% bandwidth), cache hit rate (every 1% of CDN hit rate is worth money), deleting unused data, per-team cost attribution (tags) and showback.

6. Organisation. Conway's law: architecture mirrors communication. Use stream-aligned teams (timeline, search, media, graph, safety, growth), a platform team (cells, deploys, observability, data stores), enabling teams (SRE, security). About 6 to 9 engineers per team, owning code, on-call, and cost. Team Topologies is the common reference. API contracts and ownership docs for each service, written architecture decisions (ADRs), and an architecture review for one-way doors.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying "microservices fix the org". Teams need clear ownership and platform support, not just repos.
  • A migration plan with no rollback step.

notes.title: Alternatives (branches)
notes.html:
Branch A: Cell vs giant region vs per-tenant silo

Giant cluster per region Cells Per-tenant silo
Blast radius whole region (100M+ users) 1% one tenant
Ops complexity low count, huge scale many small identical units extremely high count
Efficiency best utilisation some stranded capacity (~10%) worst
Cross-user features (global trends, search) easy need a global layer hard
Fits up to ~100M 100M to billions enterprise B2B

Choose cells and build a thin global layer (identity, trends, search federation, directory).

Branch B: Cell assignment

Hash of user id Directory (map) Geo-based
Rebalance hard easy medium
Social graph locality poor (followers span cells) can cluster by graph/community good regionally
Complexity low medium low

Choose directory with geo-aware initial placement. Cross-cell reads for follows are served via replicated post streams (as in Stage 9, now between cells).

Branch C: Chaos testing approach

Manual game days Continuous automated Both
Finds process gaps technical regressions both
Risk scheduled, supervised needs guardrails medium

Choose both: automated small blast-radius faults continuously, supervised big scenarios quarterly.

Branch D: Cost model

Build everything Buy managed Hybrid
Unit cost at 1B lowest high (per-request fees) balanced
Staff needs expert teams small medium

Choose hybrid: managed for undifferentiated parts (KMS, DNS, object storage), self-run for the hot core (timeline cache, Kafka at high volume) once spend justifies a dedicated team (rule of thumb: when the managed bill exceeds roughly 3 to 5 engineers' cost and you can run it better).

Common interview traps.

  • Choosing cells with hash by user id and later finding follower reads need cross-cell calls on every request.
  • Assuming a global feature such as trending topics is simple; it needs a separate aggregation pipeline across cells.

notes.title: What breaks next
notes.html:
1. Global features: trends, global search across cells, spam signals; need stream aggregation with sketches (HyperLogLog, count-min).
  2. The control plane becomes the new single point: cell map, deployment system, config service. Keep it static-stable (data plane keeps working with last known config).
  3. Human limits: 100 cells need automation for everything; no one SSHs into a cell.
  4. Stranded capacity: partly filled cells waste 10 to 20%; rebalance.
  5. Hot partitions inside a cell during events (a final of the World Cup); celebrity mega-accounts need dedicated handling (replicated read caches, request coalescing).
  6. Regulation and trust: new laws, audits, abuse tactics; trust and safety scale linearly with users.
  7. Beyond 1B: ML ranking cost (GPU inference) can exceed the entire serving stack; becomes the next cost frontier.

Common interview traps.

  • Making the cell router depend synchronously on a central database.

notes.title: Cost
notes.html:
Approximate monthly (very rough; true numbers depend on discounts and architecture).

Item Monthly
100 cells at about $60k/cell compute and DBs $6.0M
Media storage (11 PB/year growth, tiered, about 25 PB stored) at blended $0.008/GB $200,000 (storage) plus replication
CDN and egress: 20 PB/month at about $0.015/GB negotiated $300,000 to $1M
Search, ML ranking, spam inference (GPU) $1.0M
Observability (sampled; about 30 TB logs/day) $600,000
Security, WAF, DDoS, compliance tooling $250,000
Savings from commitments and Graviton (-30% on compute) -$1.8M
Estimated total about $7M to $9M/month, ~$0.02 per DAU/month, $7 to $9 per 1,000 registered users

Add staff cost: 1,000 engineers at about $250k loaded is $20M/month, which exceeds infrastructure; people are the biggest cost at this stage. Revenue comparison: if ARPU is $0.30 per DAU per month (ads), revenue is $120M/month, and infrastructure is under 8%.

Common interview traps.

  • Optimising infrastructure while ignoring that engineers cost more.
  • Forgetting ML inference and observability in the cost model.

notes.title: LLD view
notes.html:
// Cell router (edge, stateless)
class CellRouter(private val map: CellMap, private val health: CellHealth) {
    fun route(userId: Long): Cell {
        val cell = map.cellOf(userId)            // local cache, TTL 10 min
        return if (health.isServing(cell)) cell
               else throw ServiceUnavailable(retryAfterSec = 5)  // never reroute silently to another cell
    }
}
// Dual-write migration with a verified shadow read
class PostRepositoryMigrating implements PostRepository {
    Post get(long id) {
        Post a = oldStore.get(id);
        if (flags.shadow(id)) {
            Post b = newStore.get(id);
            if (!a.equals(b)) metrics.diff("post", id);   // do not fail the request
        }
        return flags.readNew(id) ? newStore.get(id) : a;
    }
    void put(Post p) { oldStore.put(p); try { newStore.put(p); } catch (Exception e) { dlq.send(p); } }
}
# Chaos experiment sketch (Chaos Mesh style, conceptual)
kubectl apply -f - <<EOF
kind: NetworkChaos
spec:
  action: delay
  mode: fixed-percent
  value: "5"
  delay: { latency: "200ms" }
  selector: { labelSelectors: { app: search } }
  duration: "10m"
EOF

Cost attribution via labels team, service, cell; budgets alert at 80% of forecast.

Common interview traps.

  • Swallowing errors from the new store without a DLQ: silent divergence.
  • Rerouting a failed cell's users to another cell without data; it shows empty accounts.

notes.title: Decision gravity
notes.html:
Decision Gravity Why
Cell architecture One-way door (very costly) Needs consistent data placement; retrofitting after is a multi-year migration
Cell size Semi-reversible Smaller cells can be added; merging is hard
user-to-cell directory Reversible per user Moves are online
Deploy waves, chaos program Reversible Process
Data store choices in a cell Mixed; each is a migration (see above) Dual write pattern lowers the risk
Org structure / Conway Reversible but slow (quarters)
Buy vs build Reversible with cost Exit cost grows with lock-in
Encryption and key hierarchy One-way-ish Re-encrypting PBs is slow
Compliance posture One-way (legal)

The pattern: the design decisions that fix where data lives, how it is keyed, and how it is encrypted are one-way. Everything above them (deploy, routing, cost tactics) is reversible.

Common interview traps.

  • Treating an org change as instant; it takes quarters and affects architecture.

notes.title: Concepts learned
notes.html:
• Blast radius and cell-based architecture; static stability
  • Control plane vs data plane
  • Capacity planning, headroom, forecasting, load tests
  • Migrations at scale: dual write, backfill, shadow read, wave cutover
  • Chaos engineering and game days
  • Abuse prevention, WAF, DDoS, bot detection, spam pipelines, encryption hierarchy
  • Cost engineering, unit economics, attribution
  • Conway's law, team topologies, ownership and ADRs

Common interview traps.

  • Describing chaos testing as "randomly breaking things"; it is hypothesis-driven with abort conditions.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• At 1B users the problem shifts to blast radius, cost and organisation.
  • Partition the world into about 100 cells of 10M users each; any failure or bad deploy touches about 1%. Keep shared layers thin and the control plane statically stable.
  • Deploy in waves; migrate with dual writes, throttled backfill, shadow reads and cell-by-cell cutover.
  • Plan capacity per cell with 60% utilisation, N+1 cells and event headroom; verify with load tests and continuous chaos experiments.
  • Defend with WAF, adaptive rate limits, async spam classifiers, mTLS, envelope encryption.
  • Infrastructure is about $7M to $9M/month, but people cost more; organise teams around ownership with a platform team.
  • One-way doors: cell model, data placement and keys, encryption hierarchy, compliance posture.
